Read in full before designing or changing any screen, layout, spacing, visual hierarchy, color, density, component choice, interaction state, overlay, motion, data-heavy view, or interface copy in a GPUI Kit (gpui-kit / gpui-component) application, and before reviewing UI work for design quality. Also use when asked what the design rules are, or whether a UI decision follows them.\\n---\\n\\n# GPUI Kit Design Guides\\n\\nThe guide is [references/design-guides.md](references/design-guides.md). It is\\na requirement, not inspiration. Read the guide file itself before doing UI\\nwork. Do not answer from this page, from an existing screen in the codebase, or\\nfrom training data.\\n\\nIf the file is missing, fetch `https://gpui-kit.com/docs/design-guides.md`.\\nThe guide is a verbatim copy of that page, so its link to `./coding-guides.md`\\nmeans the Coding Guides in the `gpui-kit` skill (or `https://gpui-kit.com/docs/coding-guides.md`).\\n\\n## How to read it\\n\\nRead the whole guide for a new screen or a redesign. For a narrow change, read\\n\\\"Design thesis\\\" and \\\"Start from the task\\\" first, then the section for the\\nchange. Sections, in order (`grep -n '^## ' references/design-guides.md`):\\n\\n| Section                              | Read when                                                              |\\n| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |\\n| Design thesis                        | Always                                                                 |\\n| Learning from Shadcn                 | Choosing what to borrow from web component libraries                   |\\n| Start from the task                  | Always; task hierarchy, interaction promise, what to leave out         |\\n| Visual language                      | Color, typography, spacing, radius, borders, elevation, density, icons |\\n| Layout patterns                      | Window structure, sidebars, toolbars, panels, forms, resizable regions |\\n| Components and composition           | Picking a component, composing parts, when to build a new one          |\\n| Interaction states                   | Hover, focus, pressed, selected, disabled, loading, validation, danger |\\n| Feedback and overlays                | Dialog, sheet, popover, menu, notification, tooltip, dismissal, focus  |\\n| Motion                               | Any animation or transition                                            |\\n| Designing data-heavy interfaces      | Tables, lists, trees, dashboards, dense inspectors                     |\\n| Interface language                   | Any user-facing text: labels, buttons, titles, errors, empty states    |\\n| Internationalization and platform fit | Multi-locale copy, Chinese terminology, macOS/Windows conventions     |\\n| Guidance for AI-generated interfaces | Always when an agent produces UI                                       |\\n| Accessibility checklist              | Before finishing                                                       |\\n| Design review checklist              | Before finishing; run every item against the work                     |\\n\\n## Non-negotiables\\n\\nA floor, not a substitute for the guide.\\n\\n- **Desktop before web convention.** Keyboard access, window chrome, menus,\\n  dense data views, resizable regions, persistent navigation.\\n- **`Button` vs `Link`.** `Button` for every in-app command, `ghost` or\\n  `outline` when it should read quietly. `Link` only for external URLs and\\n  email addresses.\\n- **Tokens before values.** No raw hex or `rgb(...)`; use `cx.theme()`\\n  semantic tokens and rem-based helpers. Any spacing number quoted in the guide\\n  is the current default scale, not a literal to repeat.\\n- **State must be visible.** Hover, focus, selection, disabled, loading,\\n  validation, and destructive states each need distinct, consistent treatment.\\n- **Overlays.** Escape dismisses the topmost surface and returns focus to its\\n  trigger.\\n- **Copy.** Name the object and the verb: `Delete \\\"Roadmap\\\"?` with a `Delete`\\n  button, not `Are you sure?` with `OK`.\\n\\nFinish by running the Design review checklist against the work.\\n\"}}"},{"type":"input_text","text":"[{\"name\":\"mcp__codegraph__codegraph_explore\",\"description\":\"# Codegraph — available (per-project; pass projectPath)\\n\\nCodegraph is a SQLite knowledge graph of a codebase's symbols, edges, and\\nfiles (30+ languages): one `codegraph_explore` call returns the verbatim, line-numbered source\\nof the relevant symbols PLUS the call paths between them and a blast-radius\\nsummary — replacing a grep + Read loop with one round-trip.\\n\\nThis server started somewhere with no `.codegraph/` of its own, so there is no\\ndefault project — but the tools are available and work **per project**:\\n\\n- To query a project that HAS a `.codegraph/` index (e.g. a service inside a\\n  monorepo, or a second repo), pass its path as `projectPath` to\\n  `codegraph_explore` (and any other codegraph tool). Codegraph resolves the\\n  nearest `.codegraph/` at or above that path and answers from it — for as many\\n  projects as you like in one session.\\n- For a project with no `.codegraph/`, use your built-in tools (Read/Grep/Glob)\\n  for that project. Indexing is the user's decision — don't run it yourself, but\\n  if it comes up they can run `codegraph init` in a project to enable codegraph\\n  there (a new index is picked up live, no restart).\\n\\nPRIMARY TOOL — call FIRST for almost any question OR before an edit: how does X work, architecture, a bug, where/what is X, surveying an area, or the symbols you are about to change. Returns the verbatim source of the relevant symbols grouped by file in ONE capped call (Read-equivalent — treat the shown source as already Read; do NOT re-open those files), plus the call path among them. Query can be a natural-language question OR a bag of symbol/file names. Usually the ONLY call you need — more accurate context, in far fewer tokens and round-trips than a search/Read/Grep loop.\\n\\nexec tool declaration:\\n```ts\\ndeclare const tools: { mcp__codegraph__codegraph_explore(args: {\\n  // Maximum number of files to include source code from (default: 12)\\n  maxFiles?: number;\\n  // Absolute path to the project to query (or any directory inside it) — codegraph uses the nearest .codegraph/ index at or above that path. Omit to use this session's default project. Pass it to query a second codebase, or when the server root has no index of its own (e.g. a monorepo where only sub-projects are indexed, so there is no default project).\\n  projectPath: string;\\n  // Symbol names, file names, or short code terms to explore (e.g., \\\"AuthService loginUser session-manager\\\", \\\"GraphTraverser BFS impact traversal.ts\\\"). For a flow question, name the symbols spanning the flow (e.g. \\\"mutateElement renderScene\\\"). A natural-language question works too — no prior codegraph_search needed.\\n  query: string;\\n}): Promise<CallToolResult>; };\\n```\"}]"}]
]]></tool_result>

Indexing is the user's decision — don't run it yourself, but\\n  if it comes up they can run `codegraph init` in a project to enable codegraph\\n  there (a new index is picked up live, no restart).\\n\\nPRIMARY TOOL — call FIRST for almost any question OR before an edit: how does X work, architecture, a bug, where/what is X, surveying an area, or the symbols you are about to change. Returns the verbatim source of the relevant symbols grouped by file in ONE capped call (Read-equivalent — treat the shown source as already Read; do NOT re-open those files), plus the call path among them. Query can be a natural-language question OR a bag of symbol/file names. Usually the ONLY call you need — more accurate context, in far fewer tokens and round-trips than a search/Read/Grep loop.\\n\\nexec tool declaration:\\n```ts\\ndeclare const tools: { mcp__codegraph__codegraph_explore(args: {\\n  // Maximum number of files to include source code from (default: 12)\\n  maxFiles?: number;\\n  // Absolute path to the project to query (or any directory inside it) — codegraph uses the nearest .codegraph/ index at or above that path. Omit to use this session's default project. Pass it to query a second codebase, or when the server root has no index of its own (e.g. a monorepo where only sub-projects are indexed, so there is no default project).\\n  projectPath: string;\\n  // Symbol names, file names, or short code terms to explore (e.g., \\\"AuthService loginUser session-manager\\\", \\\"GraphTraverser BFS impact traversal.ts\\\"). For a flow question, name the symbols spanning the flow (e.g. \\\"mutateElement renderScene\\\"). A natural-language question works too — no prior codegraph_search needed.\\n  query: string;\\n}): Promise<CallToolResult>; };\\n```\"}]"}]

(re-entrancy, property tests, mocking)\\n# Design Workflow\\n\\n## Establish The Real Problem\\n\\nInspect the requested screen and one nearby representative screen, relevant routes, shared components, theme tokens, package/lockfiles, and existing design guidance. Trace the main action to its result before changing its presentation. Determine whether the surface is web, a desktop webview, or native UI. Use project evidence before asking questions.\\n\\nFor substantial work, write a short working brief in the response or the project's existing design document. A new planning file is not required. Capture only what changes the design:\\n\\n- **User and job:** who is doing what, how often, and what successful completion means. Distinguish known facts from assumptions.\\n- **Decision and data:** what users compare, what requires action, record volume, value ranges, latency/freshness, and consequences of mistakes.\\n- **Context:** platform, supported window sizes/input methods, permissions, locale, existing components and brand constraints.\\n- **Scope:** the surface and behaviors being improved, contracts that must survive, and the observable result to verify.\\n\\n“Make this modern” is not enough to choose a layout. Derive a plausible concrete goal from the product, such as “make failed deployments easy to locate and retry.” State the assumption and continue with reversible work. Ask only when missing context changes a material behavior or commitment. Do not invent personas, interview results, revenue outcomes, or operating thresholds.\\n\\n## Choose Structure Before Styling\\n\\nMap the shortest understandable path from entry to outcome. Mark the information needed at each decision, the action, its feedback, and the recovery path. Preserve necessary verification steps; fewer clicks alone is not a quality metric.\\n\\nChoose content structure from the task:\\n\\n- **Monitor and respond:** exceptions, severity, ownership, freshness, immediate action.\\n- **Find and manage records:** scoped search/filters, comparable rows, detail, action, result.\\n- **Analyze:** question, measures, comparison period, dimensions, drilldown, share/export if needed.\\n- **Configure:** understandable groups, current values, consequences, save/cancel and recovery.\\n\\nHybrid products can use different structures on different routes. Do not add KPI tiles, a chart, a sidebar, tabs, or a command palette just because a dashboard template contains them. Do not delete useful data to make a screenshot calmer.\\n\\nWhen the direction is ambiguous, compare a small number of plausible arrangements against the actual task and constraints, then choose. Skip alternative mockups for a clear local repair. For an existing product, improve the responsible layout/component/token rather than introducing a parallel visual system.\\n\\n## Make Visual Intent Concrete\\n\\nName the intended density, hierarchy, and emphasis in terms that guide implementation: “compact triage rows, quiet metadata, prominent unresolved status and a stable action column.” Ground a distinctive treatment in existing brand or domain cues. A generic adjective such as “premium” does not specify behavior.\\n\\nUse [Visual system](visual-system.md) to translate that intent into the existing type, space, surface, color, and interaction roles. Do not impose a favorite font, palette, card radius, motion recipe, or theme on every project. For a website or native application, apply the relevant branch of [Accessibility and adaptation](accessibility-and-adaptation.md).\\n\\n## Implement One Complete Path\\n\\nWork from layout and shared primitives through the primary task to the states that can prevent its completion. Use realistic content early: long names, a dense dataset, missing values, extreme numbers, and constrained permissions where relevant. Label mock data; keep it out of real product claims.\\n\\nRead the applicable framework reference before selecting APIs. Use the installed component's behavior, not a visually similar homemade control. Preserve accessible names, focus behavior, URL/navigation contracts, filter semantics, field names, metric meanings, and permissions. Change those deliberately when the task requires it; explain material changes.\\n\\nPlace shared fixes where their invariant belongs. Inspect a second affected consumer when changing a shared token or primitive. Keep data loading/sorting/selection behavior consistent with the backend contract. UI presentation cannot supply authorization, concurrency protection, or truthful undo by itself.\\n\\n## Close The Loop\\n\\nUse [Verification](verification.md) before declaring the interface complete. For implementation, fix the highest-impact issues found within the authorized scope; for critique, report them. Recheck the same conditions after a change. Stop when the agreed task works, the relevant states are covered, and remaining limitations are explicit—not after a predetermined number of aesthetic passes.\\n\\nHand off the concrete improvement, why it helps the task, the rendered/interaction checks performed, and meaningful gaps. Do not claim measured usability gains without actual comparative user evidence.\\n# Forms, Feedback, And Recovery\\n\\n## Match The Form To The Decision\\n\\nGroup controls by the user's task and dependencies, not by storage schema. Use persistent visible labels, clear units, and instructions before they are needed. Explain consequential defaults. Mark required/optional fields consistently without relying only on color or an unexplained symbol. Placeholder examples can help, but disappear during entry and cannot replace labels.\\n\\nChoose the simplest suitable existing control: native text/date/select controls where they fit; a maintained combobox for a long searchable set; radio buttons when a small set benefits from visible comparison; checkboxes for independent choices. A switch usually represents an immediate on/off setting—make an explicit save model clear if the product uses one. Avoid custom controls that only imitate appearance.\\n\\nKeep dependent fields understandable as they appear/disappear. Do not silently discard entered values when a parent choice changes. For long forms, use meaningful sections and useful progression; a wizard is justified by dependencies or a genuinely staged task, not by wanting fewer fields per screenshot.\\n\\nLabel actions with the outcome: “Save notification settings” or “Archive 8 projects” can be clearer than “Submit” or “Confirm.” Provide a predictable cancel/return path. If leaving would lose meaningful work, preserve a draft or use a proportionate unsaved-work safeguard consistent with the product.\\n\\n## Validate At A Helpful Time\\n\\nAvoid errors while a person is still forming valid input. Validate on submit/continue by default; after an error, timely revalidation can help confirm the correction. Earlier checks can suit costly mistakes or async availability checks when they do not interrupt typing. Keep frontend and backend rules consistent; client checks do not replace server validation.\\n\\nAn error should identify the field/problem and a feasible repair, retain the entered values, and stay associated with its control. For a multi-field submission, a linked summary can help users find errors beyond the viewport. Focus the summary or first actionable error according to the established pattern, and expose the association programmatically. Do not announce the same error repeatedly on every render.\\n\\nSeparate invalid input from service failure, permission denial, and conflicting edits. Users cannot correct a server outage by changing a valid email address. If a record changed elsewhere, show the conflict and preserve the draft; do not overwrite quietly.\\n\\n## Specify Relevant States Before Styling Them\\n\\nUse this matrix for states the feature can actually encounter. Do not manufacture every state for a static component.\\n\\n| State | What the user needs | Common failure to prevent |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| Initial loading | What is loading; stable context and layout | Empty-state flash or false zero values |\\n| Background refresh | Retained usable data and freshness/pending cue | Blanking the screen, moving focus or rows |\\n| No records yet | Explanation and a relevant first step | Meaningless empty decoration |\\n| No matches | Applied query and a way to adjust/reset | Suggesting creation as if no data exists |\\n| Partial data | What is missing and effect on totals | Treating incomplete results as complete |\\n| Error/offline | What failed, retained work, recovery path | Clearing input or hiding the retry context |\\n| Permission/read-only | Available scope and legitimate next step | A disabled mystery control or leaked sensitive data |\\n| Submitting | Which action is pending; duplicate prevention | Multiple commits or an indefinite disabled state |\\n| Success | What changed and its scope | A short toast as the only lasting evidence |\\n| Conflict/partial success | Per-item or per-field outcomes and next step | Claiming all changes succeeded |\\n\\nUse skeletons for known structural placeholders when helpful; use concise progress feedback when the shape or duration is unknown. Do not fabricate a percentage. A refresh should retain old data only when displaying it remains safe and clearly marked. Keep refresh errors distinct from the retained data's validity.\\n\\nOptimistic updates fit reversible, low-risk actions with a reliable rollback. For destructive, financial, or uncertain operations, show a pending result until acknowledged. A timeout may mean “outcome unknown,” not “nothing happened”; check operation status before encouraging a duplicate retry. UI feedback cannot prove backend idempotency.\\n\\nChoose feedback by persistence and scope: inline near the changed field/object; a banner for a broader condition; a toast for a noncritical transient confirmation. Give critical results a durable home. Announce meaningful non-focus-taking status changes to assistive technology without announcing every poll or stealing focus.\\n\\n## Overlays And Consequential Actions\\n\\nUse a dialog for a bounded decision or short task; an anchored popover for local context; a nonmodal panel when users need to keep comparing against the underlying page. Long, nested, or independently linkable work usually deserves a page. Avoid nested modal workflows when one coherent surface can hold the task.\\n\\nUse the component library's focus management. Name the dialog, move focus appropriately on open, keep keyboard focus within a modal, make dismissal and cancellation clear, and return focus to the trigger or a sensible successor. Verify Escape/backdrop behavior does not discard work unexpectedly. Check small windows, scroll containment, sticky footers, and virtual keyboards.\\n\\nBefore a consequential action, show its target, scope, and actual consequence. Prefer an undo when real, safe reversal exists; use confirmation for irreversible/high-impact operations. A typed-name confirmation may suit rare, serious deletion; do not impose it on routine work. Keep the safe exit discoverable and the destructive action distinct without relying solely on red.\\n\\nDisabled controls need an understandable reason when it is not evident. Put the explanation in reachable text; a tooltip on an unfocusable control is insufficient. Hide restricted details when disclosure would be inappropriate, but remember that hiding a control is not authorization.\\n\\n## Proof Scenario\\n\\nEdit several values, submit one invalid field, correct it, then exercise a recoverable save failure using a safe fixture. Verify values survive, the error points to the right field, the next action is clear, and focus/status behavior works. Repeat at a constrained viewport. For a mixed bulk result, verify both the successful items and the recoverable failures remain understandable.\\n\\nBasis: GOV.UK [validation recovery](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/validation/) and [error summaries](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-summary/), WAI [labels](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/labels/), [status messages](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html), and [dialog patterns](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/). The state matrix and operation-recovery guidance are local Connect your\\nserver, choose a folder, and use your games in RetroBat or another emulator.\\nGame files download when opened and are cached for later use.\\n\\n- **RomM** stores your library on the server.\\n- **RomMFS** connects that library to this PC and keeps the games folder available.\\n- **RetroBat or your emulator** browses and plays the games.\\n\\nArtwork updates and optional save sync run alongside the games folder. Save\\nsync is off until you enable it. The project is under active development.\\n\\n## Quick start\\n\\nRequirements and detailed setup are in the [user guide](docs/user-guide.md).\\nFor a local Windows build, install Rust 1.89 or later with the MSVC toolchain\\nand Windows SDK, then run:\\n\\n```powershell\\ncargo run --locked -p rommfs-app\\n```\\n\\n1. Enter your RomM server address and choose **Sign in with browser…**.\\n   Approve the connection in RomM.\\n2. Choose an empty folder on a local NTFS drive for your games.\\n3. For RetroBat, follow **Settings → RetroBat** to connect your installation.\\n   See the [RetroBat setup guide](docs/user-guide.md#set-up-retrobat).\\n4. On **Overview**, choose **Make games available**. When the status becomes\\n   **Available**, open RetroBat or point your emulator at the games folder.\\n\\nKeep RomMFS running while you play. The first read downloads a game file;\\nlater reads use cached bytes. Game files in this folder are read-only.\\nSee [everyday use](docs/user-guide.md#everyday-use) for saves, updates, and\\nwhat the status messages mean.\\n\\n## Workspace\\n\\n| Crate | Responsibility |\\n|---|---|\\n| `rommfs-core` | RomM client, catalogue, cache, save logic, and RetroBat setup/metadata. |\\n| `rommfs-fixture` | In-process HTTP fixture used by portable tests. |\\n| `rommfs-cfapi` | Windows Cloud Files adapter and portable mount-root ownership checks. |\\n| `rommfs-app` | GPUI desktop UI, controller, session, and save-sync worker. |\\n\\n## Project docs\\n\\n- [User guide](docs/user-guide.md): requirements, Generic folders, RetroBat, save sync, and limitations.\\n- [Development guide](docs/development.md): build and check commands, crate/task map, and where tests live.\\n- [Architecture](docs/architecture.md): current crate boundaries, data flow, and invariants.\\n- [RomM API contract](docs/contracts/romm-api.md): verified and source-backed API behavior, with evidence boundaries.\\n- [Windows testing](docs/testing/windows.md): native acceptance procedure and report format.\\n- [Dated validation record](docs/validation/2026-10-12.md): implementation status and recorded Linux/Windows evidence.\\n\\n## Testing wizard\\n\\nContributors can run `test-wizard.cmd` on Windows for guided checks and local\\nevidence collection. See [Windows testing](docs/testing/windows.md) for the\\nprocedure, resume/skip controls, and screenshot privacy information.\\n# Architecture\\n\\nThis page describes the current workspace as implemented. It is a navigation\\nmap, not a target design; use the code as the authority when behavior changes.\\n\\n## Follow a user action\\n\\nFor a UI change, start in `crates/rommfs-app/src/window/pages/`. Each page reads\\n`UiState` and sends a `Command`; the window does not download games or sync saves.\\n\\nFor a behavior change, follow that command into the relevant module under\\n`crates/rommfs-app/src/controller/`. Workers report events, and\\n`controller/state.rs` turns them into the state the pages display. Shared\\nfolder, save, and artwork summaries live there so different screens agree.\\n`problem.rs` translates technical failures into explanations; the original\\nmessage remains available in the UI's technical details.\\n\\nFor example, **Make games available** sends `Command::StartMount`. The mount\\ncontroller prepares the filesystem through core and the platform adapter, then\\nreports progress and completion. **Available** comes from the completion event.\\nOpening a game later triggers its download through the filesystem; displaying\\nthe Overview does not read game contents.\\n\\n## Crate boundaries\\n\\n`rommfs-core` contains portable domain and I/O code: RomM HTTP access in\\n`romm/`, DTO-to-filesystem projection in `catalogue.rs`, path and layout rules,\\ncache/download behavior, save-sync rules and persistence, plus RetroBat setup\\nand metadata. Its filesystem facade is `filesystem.rs`; `tree.rs` provides stable\\nfilesystem enumeration from a catalogue snapshot.\\n\\n`rommfs-cfapi` separates portable root ownership and frontend metadata\\noperations (`root.rs`) from Windows CFAPI and ACL behavior (`windows.rs` and\\n`security.rs`). Native integration tests exercise a real mounted root on\\nWindows.\\n\\n`rommfs-app` owns user-facing orchestration. `controller.rs` owns controller state and worker dispatch. Focused modules in\\n`controller/` handle state/events, commands, connection, catalogue, mounting,\\nRetroBat setup, and save-sync setup. `save_sync_agent/` owns the background reconciliation and\\ntransfer actor. `window.rs` and `window/` provide the GPUI interface. The\\nsession and desktop modules own app lifetime and Windows tray/startup behavior.\\n\\n`rommfs-fixture` supplies a local HTTP server for deterministic tests. It\\nsupports assertions about requests and response bodies without requiring a\\nlive RomM instance. `route_hit_count` counts scripted route matches;\\n`request_count` counts captured wire requests.\\n\\n## Data flow\\n\\n1. The app authenticates through a `RommClient` and verifies the account when\\n   using remembered browser pairing.\\n2. It restores an account/server-scoped catalogue snapshot when available, or\\n   fetches the paginated platforms and ROM/file metadata. The first page\\n   requests the total; the remaining offsets are fetched four at a time and\\n   reassembled in offset order. A refresh is incremental when a snapshot for the\\n   same server/account exists and its last full refresh is under 24 h old:\\n   `/api/roms/identifiers` gives the authoritative visible id set and\\n   `updated_after` gives the changed ROMs, which are merged in place. A missing\\n   `/identifiers` route, a rejected `updated_after` or an unreconcilable delta\\n   falls back to a full walk. Refresh can happen in the background while the\\n   previous complete snapshot remains available.\\n3. `catalogue.rs` validates each original file identity and path, then projects\\n   supported original files into a generic or RetroBat tree. Multi-file games\\n   are represented as their individual original files when their paths are\\n   valid; unsupported or invalid records are reported.\\n4. The tree exposes placeholders. Listing is metadata-only. A content read\\n   resolves the `(server, ROM, file)` identity and downloads original bytes to\\n   the private cache as needed.\\n5. On Windows, `rommfs-cfapi` presents that filesystem through Cloud Files API.\\n   Root ownership checks and cleanup preserve unowned or modified content.\\n6. Save synchronization is a separate opt-in path. Controller configuration\\n   establishes its identity and roots; the save-sync agent observes files,\\n   reconciles local and remote revisions, and preserves conflicts for review.\\n\\n## State and ownership rules\\n\\n- A catalogue is immutable for a mounted tree. Refresh produces a new snapshot;\\n  the UI can report that a remount is needed for structural changes.\\n- Catalogue refresh has two modes. A full walk disables the unused\\n  char-index/filter-value/rom-id-index sidecars and asks for the total only on\\n  the first page; an incremental refresh merges `updated_after` against the\\n  snapshot and `/api/roms/identifiers`. The server's `updated_at` delta may not\\n  cover a rescan that only changed a ROM's file rows, so a full refresh runs at\\n  least every 24 h (`CatalogueSnapshot.full_refreshed_at`) and whenever the\\n  delta cannot be reconciled. `refreshed_at` is the refresh *start* time, so the\\n  next delta's five-minute skew covers the whole window.\\n- Real-time updates are a bounded incremental poll, not a socket client: RomM's\\n  socket.io connect handler resolves identity from the web session cookie only\\n  (the `auth` payload is ignored), so a bearer-only session cannot subscribe.\\n  The connected session arms a five-minute catalogue poll; it is cleared on\\n  sign-out and drained by the same cancellation as a manual refresh, and a\\n  stale result cannot publish into a later connection. The mounted tree stays a\\n  snapshot; the poll only stages the next one. Live play data rides the same\\n  path: a poll that lands while mounted re-runs the metadata pass, which already\\n  pulls favourites and play sessions.\\n- Catalogue snapshots are scoped by normalized server and authenticated account.\\n  Tokens remain in memory; only paired secrets use Windows Credential Manager.\\n- ROM content cache and save-sync state are separate persistence areas.\\n- Save presentation uses current per-identity work emitted by the actor, not\\n  historical transfer stages. A settled unchanged watcher hint publishes its\\n  drained queue. Retained remote review versions remain attached to their save\\n  identity and are excluded from queued-download counts. Persisted consent,\\n  checking, current transfers and last successful scan time are separate facts.\\n  See [UI remediation](ux-remediation.md) for the affected journeys and limits.\\n- Metadata setup inspection validates the managed root through the CFAPI owner\\n  before comparing its setup record. Ordinary save/setup paths still reject\\n  reparse points. Artwork publication and favourites/history failures have\\n  separate presentation state.\\n- Mount ownership is recorded beside the root. Cleanup validates ownership and\\n  does not recursively clear user data.\\n- Worker threads/tasks are owned by the app/controller lifecycle and are joined\\n  or drained on stop, logout, or quit. Cancelling a background job moves its\\n  handle to a draining list the worker loop reaps with `is_finished()`, so an\\n  in-flight HTTP request cannot stall the loop for its whole timeout; the\\n  handles are joined when the connection changes or the app shuts down.\\n  Event/session IDs prevent stale work from changing a later connection.\\n- Catalogue refresh, artwork caching, and gamelist generation/publication each\\n  run on their own thread and are polled by the worker. Gamelist publication\\n  reads and merges the RetroBat-owned gamelists, so it never blocks the loop;\\n  the mounted tree stays a snapshot and a completed refresh is applied on the\\n  next mount. A finished refresh result that waits more than five seconds to be\\n  polled is logged as a watchdog warning.\\n- The frontend metadata pass is visible: it reports a stage (\\\"Downloading\\n  artwork\\\", \\\"Writing N gamelists\\\", \\\"Artwork & gamelists up to date\\\") and artwork\\n  counts as `FrontendMetadataProgress`. These counts describe artwork checks,\\n  including cache hits, rather than the whole update. Once they finish, the UI\\n  uses an indeterminate indicator while game information is prepared and\\n  published. A blocked exclusive-access guard remains a pending wait with its\\n  diagnostic available; it is not a terminal failure or a reason to restart the\\n  update. Cancelling/stopping a pass does not advance the last-success time.\\n  Artwork uses eight bounded workers\\n  (`CONCURRENCY` in `retrobat/artwork.rs`, matching this note), and progress is\\n  throttled to about 4 Hz with the completed count only moving forward (the\\n  reporter takes the maximum under its own lock, so out-of-order worker\\n  completions cannot report a lower count). Every status and progress event\\n  carries the pass's monotonic job id; `FrontendMetadataInvalidated` marks a\\n  cancelled pass, and the UI accepts progress only for the currently active\\n  pass, so a stale artwork callback or publication status cannot revive or\\n  finish a newer pass. The log line for each status is still written even when\\n  the UI drops the event. Artwork downloads use the same `RommClient` as the\\n  catalogue; `isahc`'s `Request::send` runs on a process-global shared client, so\\n  the connection pool is reused across the artwork workers and the catalogue\\n  fetch. A cached artwork file is named by its detected extension\\n  (`.rommfs-artwork/<key>.<ext>`), so a cache hit is validated by size only and\\n  never re-reads (or re-raster-checks) the image bytes; the exact file path is\\n  still reparse-checked, not just its parent.\\n- RetroBat integration coexists with the user's own ROMs. Setup adds only a\\n  `roms/<system>/RomM` link per system and records what it owns in\\n  `.rommfs-setup.json`; it never moves, replaces or deletes existing files.\\n  An earlier-schema record is surfaced to the UI as a migration prompt rather\\n  than a mount error: Overview offers an update that reruns setup, and Start is\\n  disabled while setup or migration is pending. Rerunning setup converts the\\n  old links and restores any folders an earlier build moved aside.\\n  Gamelists are merged in place: RomMFS rewrites only its `./RomM/…` entries.\\n  Publication checks current link targets; missing or redirected links are\\n  excluded. Unreadable systems retain their identity state. Gamelist writes\\n  are attempted independently; any write failure leaves the identity index\\n  staged so a retry cannot recapture old XML against new filename mappings.\\n- Favourites and play-history sync (`romm/play_data.rs`, `retrobat/play_data.rs`)\\n  is opt-in and scoped to the verified server and account (`play_data_consent`).\\n  The metadata pass pulls the favourites collection and the account's play\\n  sessions once, reconciles each `./RomM/…` game against a per-identity baseline\\n  stored in the metadata index, and publishes the merged values; a new local\\n  launch is pushed as a play session. The first reconciliation adopts the union\\n  of both sides instead of adding two histories. A failed push keeps the local\\n  delta for the next pass. A debounced gamelist watch re-runs metadata after\\n  RetroBat writes play data, on the metadata thread and under the same\\n  stopped-RetroBat guard.\\n- \\\"Hide RomM games you already have\\\" is on by default and runs in the metadata\\n  pass (`retrobat/owned.rs`). It reads the user's own files in `roms/<system>/`\\n  read-only, matching by name-without-extension and exact size, then confirming\\n  under a 512 MB cap with whichever of CRC32, MD5 or SHA-1 RomM provides; above\\n  the cap name and size are enough. The `RomM` folder is skipped by name even\\n  when it is a real directory, and a linked system root or a linked `roms` root\\n  is never followed. A file the user can't read never matches, so nothing is\\n  inferred from an unreadable path. Local hashes are cached in the per-server\\n  cache by path, size and nanosecond modification time. A system that can't be\\n  read is reported and left visible. Ownership of the gamelist `hidden` flag is\\n  recorded per identity in the metadata index (`auto_hidden`), so removing a\\n  local copy, or turning the switch off, unhides only what RomMFS hid — a\\n  `hidden` the user set, and play-data history, are never touched. Play-data\\n  sync carries `hidden` verbatim and never pushes it to RomM.\\n- Save-sync consent and journal state are separate from mount configuration.\\n  Paths, scopes, and identities are validated before reads or writes.\\n- Memory-card sync (`save_sync/memory_cards.rs`, `save_sync/memory_card_journal.rs`,\\n  `save_sync_agent/memory_cards.rs`, `romm/memory_cards.rs`) is a separate sync\\n  kind next to ordinary saves. A card's identity is (server, account, emulator,\\n  card name); its durable baseline is the accepted RomM version id plus the hash\\n  of the local card (`MemoryCardJournal`, in the save-sync journal DB). Discovery\\n  reads only the two RetroBat `memcards` folders (`psx/duckstation/memcards`,\\n  `ps2/pcsx2/memcards`); a card is a `*.mcd`/`*.ps2` file or, for PCSX2, a\\n  folder. Consent is off by default and scoped per discovered card folder\\n  (`memory_card_consent`), like a save root. The card reconciliation thread is\\n  owned by `SaveSyncAgent` (its start/stop/drop lifecycle), so it also runs when\\n  save sync itself is off; it keeps its own polling cadence because a 256 MB\\n  transfer must not block the save actor. It reuses `SaveSyncScope`/\\n  `SaveSyncIdentity`, the consent store, and the emulator guard. The guard\\n  enumerates the executables inside each installed DuckStation/PCSX2 folder and\\n  opens them exclusively (rather than guessing names); an installed folder with\\n  no executable, or any open image, means nothing syncs — the reason is\\n  reported, never a silent pass. It also waits for the quiet period before an\\n  upload. A consented folder is enumerated even when empty, so a card that\\n  exists only on RomM (synced from another machine) is restored; the archive\\n  layout is inferred (a single top-level file with the emulator's own extension\\n  restores as a file, anything else as a folder for PCSX2) and the\\n  server-supplied name is validated first. Uploads are bounded, safe zips\\n  (≤256 MB). An unreadable card, a reparse point, or a folder card containing a\\n  reparse point is rejected, never treated as absent or silently truncated.\\n  Before a download replaces a card the worker rechecks cancellation and the\\n  local baseline, and refuses if the destination exists at all (even\\n  unreadable), so a concurrent local edit becomes a conflict, never an\\n  overwrite. A conflict keeps the local card and writes the remote beside it as\\n  a version-specific `.rommfs-conflict-v<id>` sibling, so every reported remote\\n  version is actually preserved; the card is listed in Save review. Archive\\n  entry paths are validated per component with the same Windows-name validator\\n  used for save targets. The `memcards` exclusion for ordinary per-game save\\n  mapping remains in force.\\n\\nFor user-facing restrictions, see the [user guide](user-guide.md). For the\\nsource and confidence level of RomM route assumptions, see the [API contract](contracts/romm-api.md).\\n# Development guide\\n\\nThis guide is for contributors and agents making changes in the workspace.\\nFor product setup, see the [user guide](user-guide.md). For module ownership\\nand behavior, see [architecture](architecture.md).\\n\\n## Build and checks\\n\\nUse Rust 1.89 or later. Building the Windows desktop app and CFAPI adapter\\nrequires the MSVC Rust target, Visual Studio C++ build tools, and Windows SDK.\\nPortable core, fixture, and headless app checks run on Linux, macOS, and Windows.\\n\\nFrom the repository root:\\n\\n```sh\\ncargo fmt --all --check\\ncargo test --locked -p rommfs-core -p rommfs-fixture -p rommfs-cfapi -p rommfs-app --no-default-features -- --test-threads=1\\ncargo clippy --locked -p rommfs-core -p rommfs-fixture -p rommfs-cfapi -p rommfs-app --no-default-features --all-targets -- -D warnings\\ncargo check --locked -p rommfs-app --all-targets\\n```\\n\\nThe optional mise aliases are `mise run test:portable` for the headless suite,\\n`mise run check:ui` for host-native UI compilation, and `mise run test:native`\\nfor the Windows workspace suite. `test:native` refuses to run on non-Windows\\nhosts. The direct equivalents are shown above and below; mise is not required.\\n\\nOn Windows, `cargo test --locked --workspace -- --test-threads=1` exercises UI\\nand native CFAPI tests. The native acceptance procedure, including live and\\nmanual cases, is in [Windows testing](testing/windows.md). Compilation and\\nportable fixtures do not establish native runtime behavior.\\n\\n## GPUI MCP automation\\n\\nFor local agent-driven UI checks, run the opt-in debug build:\\n\\n```powershell\\nmise x -- mbx run --locked -p rommfs-app --features mcp\\n```\\n\\nAppend `-- --mcp-background` to open the automation window without requesting\\ndesktop focus. (re-entrancy, property tests, mocking)\\n# Design Workflow\\n\\n## Establish The Real Problem\\n\\nInspect the requested screen and one nearby representative screen, relevant routes, shared components, theme tokens, package/lockfiles, and existing design guidance. Trace the main action to its result before changing its presentation. Determine whether the surface is web, a desktop webview, or native UI. Use project evidence before asking questions.\\n\\nFor substantial work, write a short working brief in the response or the project's existing design document. A new planning file is not required. Capture only what changes the design:\\n\\n- **User and job:** who is doing what, how often, and what successful completion means. Distinguish known facts from assumptions.\\n- **Decision and data:** what users compare, what requires action, record volume, value ranges, latency/freshness, and consequences of mistakes.\\n- **Context:** platform, supported window sizes/input methods, permissions, locale, existing components and brand constraints.\\n- **Scope:** the surface and behaviors being improved, contracts that must survive, and the observable result to verify.\\n\\n“Make this modern” is not enough to choose a layout. Derive a plausible concrete goal from the product, such as “make failed deployments easy to locate and retry.” State the assumption and continue with reversible work. Ask only when missing context changes a material behavior or commitment. Do not invent personas, interview results, revenue outcomes, or operating thresholds.\\n\\n## Choose Structure Before Styling\\n\\nMap the shortest understandable path from entry to outcome. Mark the information needed at each decision, the action, its feedback, and the recovery path. Preserve necessary verification steps; fewer clicks alone is not a quality metric.\\n\\nChoose content structure from the task:\\n\\n- **Monitor and respond:** exceptions, severity, ownership, freshness, immediate action.\\n- **Find and manage records:** scoped search/filters, comparable rows, detail, action, result.\\n- **Analyze:** question, measures, comparison period, dimensions, drilldown, share/export if needed.\\n- **Configure:** understandable groups, current values, consequences, save/cancel and recovery.\\n\\nHybrid products can use different structures on different routes. Do not add KPI tiles, a chart, a sidebar, tabs, or a command palette just because a dashboard template contains them. Do not delete useful data to make a screenshot calmer.\\n\\nWhen the direction is ambiguous, compare a small number of plausible arrangements against the actual task and constraints, then choose. Skip alternative mockups for a clear local repair. For an existing product, improve the responsible layout/component/token rather than introducing a parallel visual system.\\n\\n## Make Visual Intent Concrete\\n\\nName the intended density, hierarchy, and emphasis in terms that guide implementation: “compact triage rows, quiet metadata, prominent unresolved status and a stable action column.” Ground a distinctive treatment in existing brand or domain cues. A generic adjective such as “premium” does not specify behavior.\\n\\nUse [Visual system](visual-system.md) to translate that intent into the existing type, space, surface, color, and interaction roles. Do not impose a favorite font, palette, card radius, motion recipe, or theme on every project. For a website or native application, apply the relevant branch of [Accessibility and adaptation](accessibility-and-adaptation.md).\\n\\n## Implement One Complete Path\\n\\nWork from layout and shared primitives through the primary task to the states that can prevent its completion. Use realistic content early: long names, a dense dataset, missing values, extreme numbers, and constrained permissions where relevant. Label mock data; keep it out of real product claims.\\n\\nRead the applicable framework reference before selecting APIs. Use the installed component's behavior, not a visually similar homemade control. Preserve accessible names, focus behavior, URL/navigation contracts, filter semantics, field names, metric meanings, and permissions. Change those deliberately when the task requires it; explain material changes.\\n\\nPlace shared fixes where their invariant belongs. Inspect a second affected consumer when changing a shared token or primitive. Keep data loading/sorting/selection behavior consistent with the backend contract. UI presentation cannot supply authorization, concurrency protection, or truthful undo by itself.\\n\\n## Close The Loop\\n\\nUse [Verification](verification.md) before declaring the interface complete. For implementation, fix the highest-impact issues found within the authorized scope; for critique, report them. Recheck the same conditions after a change. Stop when the agreed task works, the relevant states are covered, and remaining limitations are explicit—not after a predetermined number of aesthetic passes.\\n\\nHand off the concrete improvement, why it helps the task, the rendered/interaction checks performed, and meaningful gaps. Do not claim measured usability gains without actual comparative user evidence.\\n# Forms, Feedback, And Recovery\\n\\n## Match The Form To The Decision\\n\\nGroup controls by the user's task and dependencies, not by storage schema. Use persistent visible labels, clear units, and instructions before they are needed. Explain consequential defaults. Mark required/optional fields consistently without relying only on color or an unexplained symbol. Placeholder examples can help, but disappear during entry and cannot replace labels.\\n\\nChoose the simplest suitable existing control: native text/date/select controls where they fit; a maintained combobox for a long searchable set; radio buttons when a small set benefits from visible comparison; checkboxes for independent choices. A switch usually represents an immediate on/off setting—make an explicit save model clear if the product uses one. Avoid custom controls that only imitate appearance.\\n\\nKeep dependent fields understandable as they appear/disappear. Do not silently discard entered values when a parent choice changes. For long forms, use meaningful sections and useful progression; a wizard is justified by dependencies or a genuinely staged task, not by wanting fewer fields per screenshot.\\n\\nLabel actions with the outcome: “Save notification settings” or “Archive 8 projects” can be clearer than “Submit” or “Confirm.” Provide a predictable cancel/return path. If leaving would lose meaningful work, preserve a draft or use a proportionate unsaved-work safeguard consistent with the product.\\n\\n## Validate At A Helpful Time\\n\\nAvoid errors while a person is still forming valid input. Validate on submit/continue by default; after an error, timely revalidation can help confirm the correction. Earlier checks can suit costly mistakes or async availability checks when they do not interrupt typing. Keep frontend and backend rules consistent; client checks do not replace server validation.\\n\\nAn error should identify the field/problem and a feasible repair, retain the entered values, and stay associated with its control. For a multi-field submission, a linked summary can help users find errors beyond the viewport. Focus the summary or first actionable error according to the established pattern, and expose the association programmatically. Do not announce the same error repeatedly on every render.\\n\\nSeparate invalid input from service failure, permission denial, and conflicting edits. Users cannot correct a server outage by changing a valid email address. If a record changed elsewhere, show the conflict and preserve the draft; do not overwrite quietly.\\n\\n## Specify Relevant States Before Styling Them\\n\\nUse this matrix for states the feature can actually encounter. Do not manufacture every state for a static component.\\n\\n| State | What the user needs | Common failure to prevent |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| Initial loading | What is loading; stable context and layout | Empty-state flash or false zero values |\\n| Background refresh | Retained usable data and freshness/pending cue | Blanking the screen, moving focus or rows |\\n| No records yet | Explanation and a relevant first step | Meaningless empty decoration |\\n| No matches | Applied query and a way to adjust/reset | Suggesting creation as if no data exists |\\n| Partial data | What is missing and effect on totals | Treating incomplete results as complete |\\n| Error/offline | What failed, retained work, recovery path | Clearing input or hiding the retry context |\\n| Permission/read-only | Available scope and legitimate next step | A disabled mystery control or leaked sensitive data |\\n| Submitting | Which action is pending; duplicate prevention | Multiple commits or an indefinite disabled state |\\n| Success | What changed and its scope | A short toast as the only lasting evidence |\\n| Conflict/partial success | Per-item or per-field outcomes and next step | Claiming all changes succeeded |\\n\\nUse skeletons for known structural placeholders when helpful; use concise progress feedback when the shape or duration is unknown. Do not fabricate a percentage. A refresh should retain old data only when displaying it remains safe and clearly marked. Keep refresh errors distinct from the retained data's validity.\\n\\nOptimistic updates fit reversible, low-risk actions with a reliable rollback. For destructive, financial, or uncertain operations, show a pending result until acknowledged. A timeout may mean “outcome unknown,” not “nothing happened”; check operation status before encouraging a duplicate retry. UI feedback cannot prove backend idempotency.\\n\\nChoose feedback by persistence and scope: inline near the changed field/object; a banner for a broader condition; a toast for a noncritical transient confirmation. Give critical results a durable home. Announce meaningful non-focus-taking status changes to assistive technology without announcing every poll or stealing focus.\\n\\n## Overlays And Consequential Actions\\n\\nUse a dialog for a bounded decision or short task; an anchored popover for local context; a nonmodal panel when users need to keep comparing against the underlying page. Long, nested, or independently linkable work usually deserves a page. Avoid nested modal workflows when one coherent surface can hold the task.\\n\\nUse the component library's focus management. Name the dialog, move focus appropriately on open, keep keyboard focus within a modal, make dismissal and cancellation clear, and return focus to the trigger or a sensible successor. Verify Escape/backdrop behavior does not discard work unexpectedly. Check small windows, scroll containment, sticky footers, and virtual keyboards.\\n\\nBefore a consequential action, show its target, scope, and actual consequence. Prefer an undo when real, safe reversal exists; use confirmation for irreversible/high-impact operations. A typed-name confirmation may suit rare, serious deletion; do not impose it on routine work. Keep the safe exit discoverable and the destructive action distinct without relying solely on red.\\n\\nDisabled controls need an understandable reason when it is not evident. Put the explanation in reachable text; a tooltip on an unfocusable control is insufficient. Hide restricted details when disclosure would be inappropriate, but remember that hiding a control is not authorization.\\n\\n## Proof Scenario\\n\\nEdit several values, submit one invalid field, correct it, then exercise a recoverable save failure using a safe fixture. Verify values survive, the error points to the right field, the next action is clear, and focus/status behavior works. Repeat at a constrained viewport. For a mixed bulk result, verify both the successful items and the recoverable failures remain understandable.\\n\\nBasis: GOV.UK [validation recovery](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/validation/) and [error summaries](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/components/error-summary/), WAI [labels](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/forms/labels/), [status messages](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html), and [dialog patterns](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/). The state matrix and operation-recovery guidance are local It records\\nthe product judgment accumulated through years of GPUI Kit desktop work:\\nan interface should feel native, restrained, precise, and understandable\\nwithout guesswork.\\n\\nThis is a normative guide. **Must** identifies a correctness or ecosystem\\nconstraint, **should** is the default that needs a concrete reason to override,\\nand **may** is an optional technique. Component API documentation remains the\\nauthority for individual methods.\\n\\nThe rules build on behavior in `gpui-base`, the GPUI Component theme and\\ncomponent system, and familiar desktop interaction. When influences conflict, preserve GPUI's\\nlifecycle constraints and the interaction people already understand.\\n\\n## Design thesis\\n\\nBuild interfaces that feel native, quiet, and precise. Create a new primitive only\\n   when its behavior is genuinely new.\\n3. **Tokens before values.** Colors, radii, typography, and spacing should form\\n   a system. Avoid isolated literals that cannot respond to themes.\\n4. **Desktop before web convention.** Preserve keyboard access, window chrome,\\n   menus, dense data views, resizable regions, and persistent navigation where\\n   the task benefits from them.\\n5. **State must be visible.** Hover, focus, selection, disabled, loading,\\n   validation, and destructive states need distinct and consistent treatment.\\n6. **Geometry explains containment.** Radii, insets, and boundaries should\\n   describe one coherent hierarchy, even where surfaces overlap.\\n7. **Feedback reflects reality.** Loading, tooltips, and motion should clarify\\n   a real state or transition, not add ceremony to an immediate action.\\n\\n## Learning from Shadcn\\n\\nShadcn's most useful contribution is not a particular border color. It is a\\nway of building a system:\\n\\n- own the top layer of the interface instead of fighting a sealed abstraction;\\n- compose small, predictable parts into product-specific components;\\n- provide defaults that already form one visual language;\\n- keep the code and composition legible to both people and AI;\\n- separate behavior primitives from the styled layer.\\n\\nGPUI Kit applies those ideas through a Rust library and the split between\\n`gpui-base` and `gpui-component`. Applications normally compose or wrap the\\npublished components; contributors move genuinely reusable behavior into Base\\nand keep visual policy above it.\\n\\nDo not copy these web assumptions blindly:\\n\\n| Web habit | Native GPUI default |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Pointing-hand cursor on every button | Default arrow cursor; pointing hand for links |\\n| Page navigation as the main structure | Persistent windows, panes, sidebars, tabs, and menus |\\n| Browser focus and scrolling as a fallback | Explicit focus ownership and region-owned scrolling |\\n| Mobile-first single column | Resizable desktop shell with a defined minimum window size |\\n| Hover-revealed critical actions | Keyboard- and pointer-reachable actions that do not depend on hover |\\n| A row of hover-only icon buttons | A visible primary action plus `DropdownMenu` or `ContextMenu` for secondary commands |\\n| Link-styled text for application commands | `Button`, `outline`, or `ghost`; Link only for URLs, web resources, or email addresses |\\n| Large touch density everywhere | Medium density by default; compact only where information work benefits |\\n| CSS overrides across descendants | Typed builders, semantic parts, and application composition |\\n\\n## Start from the task\\n\\nBefore drawing a screen, write down:\\n\\n- the user's primary task;\\n- the object being viewed or changed;\\n- the actions that must remain immediately available;\\n- the information required to make a decision;\\n- empty, loading, error, offline, read-only, and permission-denied states;\\n- the keyboard path through the workflow.\\n\\nOrganize the window around those answers. Do not begin with a dashboard grid or\\na component catalogue. A good desktop interface exposes the user's mental\\nmodel: documents, accounts, projects, messages, settings, or another stable\\nobject—not the internal service architecture.\\n\\nDesign the primary task before distributing controls. Its visual weight,\\nlocation, and information depth should match its importance to the product. A\\ncore result must not be reduced to a small count, an icon in a corner, or a\\nweak footer action while secondary content consumes the page. [{"type":"input_text","text":"Script completed\nWall time 0.7 seconds\nOutput:\n"},{"type":"input_text","text":"Warning: truncated output (original token count: 42359)\nTotal output lines: 4\n\n{\"i\":0,\"status\":\"fulfilled\",\"value\":{\"chunk_id\":\"e866cb\",\"wall_time_seconds\":0.000017863,\"exit_code\":0,\"original_token_count\":12727,\"output\":\"---\\ntitle: Design Guides\\ndescription: Product and interaction design guidance for GPUI Kit applications\\norder: -2.1\\n---\\n\\n# Design Guides\\n\\nUse this guide before choosing components or writing layout code. It records\\nthe product judgment accumulated through years of GPUI Kit desktop work:\\nan interface should feel native, restrained, precise, and understandable\\nwithout guesswork.\\n\\nThis is a normative guide. **Must** identifies a correctness or ecosystem\\nconstraint, **should** is the default that needs a concrete reason to override,\\nand **may** is an optional technique. Component API documentation remains the\\nauthority for individual methods.\\n\\nThe rules build on behavior in `gpui-base`, the GPUI Component theme and\\ncomponent system, and familiar desktop interaction. Shadcn contributes useful\\nmethods—open code, composition, and dependable defaults—but does not determine\\nhow a GPUI application should look. When influences conflict, preserve GPUI's\\nlifecycle constraints and the interaction people already understand.\\n\\n## Design thesis\\n\\nBuild interfaces that feel native, quiet, and precise. Let content, hierarchy,\\nand interaction carry the experience; decoration should support them rather\\nthan compete with them.\\n\\n1. **Clarity before personality.** Make the primary task and next action clear\\n   before adding brand expression.\\n2. **Composition before invention.** Start with established components and\\n   compose them into product-specific workflows. Create a new primitive only\\n   when its behavior is genuinely new.\\n3. **Tokens before values.** Colors, radii, typography, and spacing should form\\n   a system. Avoid isolated literals that cannot respond to themes.\\n4. **Desktop before web convention.** Preserve keyboard access, window chrome,\\n   menus, dense data views, resizable regions, and persistent navigation where\\n   the task benefits from them.\\n5. **State must be visible.** Hover, focus, selection, disabled, loading,\\n   validation, and destructive states need distinct and consistent treatment.\\n6. **Geometry explains containment.** Radii, insets, and boundaries should\\n   describe one coherent hierarchy, even where surfaces overlap.\\n7. **Feedback reflects reality.** Loading, tooltips, and motion should clarify\\n   a real state or transition, not add ceremony to an immediate action.\\n\\n## Learning from Shadcn\\n\\nShadcn's most useful contribution is not a particular border color. It is a\\nway of building a system:\\n\\n- own the top layer of the interface instead of fighting a sealed abstraction;\\n- compose small, predictable parts into product-specific components;\\n- provide defaults that already form one visual language;\\n- keep the code and composition legible to both people and AI;\\n- separate behavior primitives from the styled layer.\\n\\nGPUI Kit applies those ideas through a Rust library and the split between\\n`gpui-base` and `gpui-component`. Applications normally compose or wrap the\\npublished components; contributors move genuinely reusable behavior into Base\\nand keep visual policy above it.\\n\\nDo not copy these web assumptions blindly:\\n\\n| Web habit | Native GPUI default |\\n| --- | --- |\\n| Pointing-hand cursor on every button | Default arrow cursor; pointing hand for links |\\n| Page navigation as the main structure | Persistent windows, panes, sidebars, tabs, and menus |\\n| Browser focus and scrolling as a fallback | Explicit focus ownership and region-owned scrolling |\\n| Mobile-first single column | Resizable desktop shell with a defined minimum window size |\\n| Hover-revealed critical actions | Keyboard- and pointer-reachable actions that do not depend on hover |\\n| A row of hover-only icon buttons | A visible primary action plus `DropdownMenu` or `ContextMenu` for secondary commands |\\n| Link-styled text for application commands | `Button`, `outline`, or `ghost`; Link only for URLs, web resources, or email addresses |\\n| Large touch density everywhere | Medium density by default; compact only where information work benefits |\\n| CSS overrides across descendants | Typed builders, semantic parts, and application composition |\\n\\n## Start from the task\\n\\nBefore drawing a screen, write down:\\n\\n- the user's primary task;\\n- the object being viewed or changed;\\n- the actions that must remain immediately available;\\n- the information required to make a decision;\\n- empty, loading, error, offline, read-only, and permission-denied states;\\n- the keyboard path through the workflow.\\n\\nOrganize the window around those answers. Do not begin with a dashboard grid or\\na component catalogue. A good desktop interface exposes the user's mental\\nmodel: documents, accounts, projects, messages, settings, or another stable\\nobject—not the internal service architecture.\\n\\nDesign the primary task before distributing controls. Its visual weight,\\nlocation, and information depth should match its importance to the product. A\\ncore result must not be reduced to a small count, an icon in a corner, or a\\nweak footer action while secondary content consumes the page. When a result set\\nis the product's main value, consider a summary region or card that exposes the\\ncount, representative results, meaningful state, and a clear next action.\\n\\nFor every proposed action, name its visible object, current state, scope, and\\nresult. If the interface does not show or clearly imply those things, the\\naction is premature. Do not expose a capability merely because the backend has\\nit; first design how the object enters the user's mental model.\\n\\n## Visual language\\n\\n### Hierarchy\\n\\nPrefer a small number of clear levels:\\n\\n- **window or page title** identifies the current object or workspace;\\n- **section title** separates meaningful regions;\\n- **body text** carries the work;\\n- **muted text** provides secondary metadata and help;\\n- **labels** identify controls and values.\\n\\nUse size, weight, spacing, and separators before adding color or containers.\\nAvoid nesting cards inside cards: most desktop regions need only a background,\\na hairline boundary, and intentional spacing.\\n\\nEvaluate hierarchy across the whole feature, not component by component. Hide\\naccent color and decoration during review: the primary task, current selection,\\nresult summary, and next action should still be obvious from structure. A\\nscreen that contains individually plausible controls can still fail when they\\ndo not form one reading order and one decision path.\\n\\nTreat emphasis as a limited budget. A local surface needs one clear focal point,\\nnot a field of competing highlights. If everything is colored, badged, bold,\\nboxed, or promoted to an alert, nothing reads as important. Establish priority\\nwith structure and proximity first; spend stronger color and components only\\nwhere a distinction changes what the user notices or does.\\n\\n### Color and themes\\n\\nRead colors from `cx.theme()` and use them by semantic role:\\n\\n- `background` and `foreground` for the main surface and text;\\n- `group_box`, `popover`, `sidebar`, and their foreground tokens for their\\n  named surfaces;\\n- `muted` and `muted_foreground` for supporting information;\\n- `primary` for the principal action or selection emphasis;\\n- `danger`, `warning`, `success`, and `info` only for their meanings;\\n- `border`, `input`, and focus-ring tokens for structure and interaction.\\n\\nDo not use a semantic status color as decoration. Do not encode meaning by\\ncolor alone. Verify every custom surface in light and dark themes and with\\ncustom theme values; never assume that foreground is black or background is\\nwhite.\\n\\nUse Badge for a short state, count, or classification that benefits from rapid\\nscanning—not for every label, metadata value, filter, or section title. Keep\\nmost badges neutral; reserve semantic variants for states that truly carry\\nsuccess, warning, danger, or informational meaning. A row of multicolored\\nbadges is usually a missing hierarchy or grouping decision.\\n\\nApplication UI should not contain raw hex, `rgb`/`rgba`, or `hsla` colors.\\nResolve colors from `cx.theme()` by semantic role. If the required role does\\nnot exist, define it in the product's theme/token layer rather than embedding a\\npalette value at the call site. Raw colors belong only inside theme definitions\\nor in audited data/raster content whose color is itself the data.\\n\\n### Radius, spacing, and density\\n\\nUse a finite radius scale, as with type and control sizes. Choose from the\\ntheme's named tiers (`sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, and larger surface tiers) instead\\nof inventing a radius for each element. Large containers may use a softer tier\\nthan the controls they contain; compact controls and overlays use tighter\\ntiers. For an ordinary rectangle, the radius should remain visibly smaller\\nthan half its shorter side. Use `radius_full()` only for intentional circles\\nand pills; a tooltip must not become a capsule by accident.\\n\\nNested surfaces should read as concentric shapes. Use\\n`inner radius ≈ max(0, outer radius − gap)` to choose the closest suitable\\ntheme tier; the visible band should remain even through the turn. Add a\\nnamed application token if a repeated composition needs an intermediate\\nvalue. A segmented control is one silhouette: its end segments follow the container's inner\\ncorners, its middle segments remain square, and each boundary has one divider\\nof consistent thickness.\\n\\n<img class=\\\"alignment-light\\\" src=\\\"/radius-hierarchy.svg\\\" alt=\\\"Light theme chat composer: the inset surface, both buttons, and placeholder spacing change together; red guide circles show their shared corner center.\\\">\\n<img class=\\\"alignment-dark\\\" src=\\\"/radius-hierarchy-dark.svg\\\" alt=\\\"Dark theme chat composer: the inset surface, both buttons, and placeholder spacing change together; red guide circles show their shared corner center.\\\">\\n\\nA radius must govern the entire visible surface, not just its border. Exposed\\ncorners remain transparent to the surface behind them; child backgrounds,\\nselection fills, and scrolling content must also follow the boundary. In GPUI,\\ndo not assume a rounded parent clips its descendants. Give inner surfaces their\\nown radius or an appropriate clip, then inspect the composition against a\\ncontrasting background in both themes. Preserve outward focus rings when\\nchoosing a clip.\\n\\nUse a compact spacing scale and repeat it. Related label/control pairs should\\nbe closer than separate groups; separate groups should be closer than separate\\nsections. Prefer component sizes (`xsmall`, `small`, default medium, `large`)\\nover one-off heights. Use compact variants for toolbars and data-dense screens,\\nnot to squeeze an unclear layout into less space.\\n\\nThe shared semantic scale is intentionally small: spacing progresses through\\nroughly 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, and 32 pixels, while typography stays near 12,\\n14, 16, 18, and 20 pixels. Treat these as relationships rather than permission\\nto scatter their current values through feature code. GPUI Component currently\\nprojects a fixed default `SpacingTokens` scale from its global `Theme`; unlike\\ncolors and radii, `Theme::apply_semantic_tokens` does not persist a custom\\nspacing scale. An application that needs different spacing must own that full\\ntoken snapshot and use it consistently in its application components.\\n\\n### Spatial grammar\\n\\nSpacing expresses relationship. Choose a gap from the semantic scale by asking\\nwhat the two things mean to each other:\\n\\n| Relationship | Typical token | Current scale | Examples |\\n| --- | --- | --- | --- |\\n| Optical correction | `xxs` | 2 px | icon baseline, compact separator |\\n| Parts of one control | `xs` | 4 px | menu icon/label, title/description |\\n| Closely related controls | `sm` | 8 px | button icon/label, dialog actions |\\n| One content group | `md` | 12 px | notification columns, compact form rows |\\n| Separate groups in one section | `lg` | 16 px | panel padding, form groups |\\n| Separate sections | `xl` | 24 px | major blocks in a page or inspector |\\n| Major region boundary | `xxl` | 32 px | empty-state breathing room, page bands |\\n\\nThese values describe the current default scale, not literals to repeat. Use\\n`cx.theme().spacing_tokens()` or the corresponding GPUI scale helpers for the\\necosystem default. A product-owned scale should preserve the ordering and\\nrelationships and must be passed through the application's own design-system\\ncontext rather than assumed to persist in the global GPUI Component theme.\\n\\nUse these rules when resolving horizontal and vertical space:\\n\\n1. **Inside before outside.** A component's padding belongs to the component;\\n   the gap between components belongs to their parent.\\n2. **Vertical rhythm shows grouping.** The gap between a title and its\\n   description is smaller than the gap from that description to the next\\n   section. Equal gaps imply equal relationships.\\n3. **Horizontal space supports scanning.** Repeated rows keep icons, labels,\\n   values, badges, and trailing actions on stable columns.\\n4. **Leading and trailing are semantic.** Think in reading-order edges even\\n   when the current API uses left/right; this keeps future RTL adaptation\\n   possible.\\n5. **Do not double padding.** A card placed in an already padded panel should\\n   not automatically add another full panel inset.\\n6. **Use optical alignment sparingly.** A one- or two-pixel correction is valid\\n   for icon or glyph geometry, but document why it differs from the scale.\\n\\nCommon compositions in the current system illustrate the relationships:\\n\\n- button contents use 4 px at small sizes and 8 px at normal sizes;\\n- dialog headers and footers use an 8 px internal gap;\\n- compact list and menu rows use 4 px vertical and 8–12 px horizontal padding;\\n- sheet headers use about 16 px leading and 12 px trailing space, leaving room\\n  for a close affordance, while footers use 16 px horizontal and 12 px vertical\\n  space;\\n- notifications use 16 px horizontal padding and a 12 px column gap because\\n  icon, message, and action are distinct groups.\\n\\nDo not treat these as copy-and-paste recipes for every surface. They reveal the\\nsystem: controls are tighter internally, rows optimize scanning, and\\ncontainers spend more space at their boundary than between their contents.\\n\\n### Proportion and layer hierarchy\\n\\nStart with content requirements, then set proportions. Avoid arbitrary halves\\nwhen one pane has a clearly different role.\\n\\n- A navigation sidebar should be wide enough for stable labels but visibly\\n  subordinate to the work area. Give it a minimum, preferred, and maximum\\n  width rather than a percentage alone.\\n- In master–detail layouts, let the collection remain scannable and give the\\n  detail pane the surplus. A roughly one-third/two-thirds starting point is\\n  often useful, but content constraints are authoritative.\\n- Inspectors and auxiliary sheets should not cover the primary object by\\n  default. They should be resizable or dismissible when their content grows.\\n- Dialog width comes from the decision: short confirmation, medium form, or a\\n  dedicated window/page for complex work. Do not enlarge a dialog simply to\\n  create whitespace.\\n- Reserve the strongest elevation for the topmost decision layer. Within a\\n  layer, use background and hairlines—not successively larger shadows—to show\\n  hierarchy.\\n\\nDefine three size constraints for every major region: the minimum at which its\\ntask still works, a comfortable default, and how it consumes surplus. Persist\\nuser-controlled splits when they represent workflow preference, and clamp\\nrestored values against the current window.\\n\\n### Alignment details\\n\\nAlignment is a structural system, not a final polish pass. Establish a small\\nset of alignment spines for each surface: shared leading and trailing edges,\\ntext baselines, center lines, and fixed functional lanes. Elements at the same\\nlevel should attach to the same spine from top to bottom or leading to trailing,\\neven when they are different component types.\\n\\n<img class=\\\"alignment-light\\\" src=\\\"/alignment-spines.svg?v=20260822-4\\\" alt=\\\"Alignment spines across a desktop surface\\\">\\n<img class=\\\"alignment-dark\\\" src=\\\"/alignment-spines-dark.svg?v=20260822-4\\\" alt=\\\"Alignment spines across a desktop surface\\\">\\n\\nVertical red lines sit beside shared edges or control centers for content,\\nstatus, time, and trailing actions. Horizontal lines sit beneath text baselines\\nor pass through a row center to show bottom and vertical-center alignment. The\\ncompact comparison isolates a one-rendered-pixel drift that must be corrected\\nat its structural owner.\\n\\n- Give sibling regions a shared content inset. A heading, toolbar, list row,\\n  empty state, and footer that describe the same level should not each invent a\\n  slightly different leading edge.\\n- Repeat column geometry through the whole region. Headers, rows, summaries,\\n  loading states, and inline editors should reserve the same lanes for identity,\\n  metadata, status, numbers, and actions.\\n- Align related controls across rows and sections. Form labels, fields,\\n  descriptions, and validation messages should reveal a stable vertical grid\\n  when the page is scanned from top to bottom.\\n- Keep horizontal bands coherent. Items sharing a toolbar, title bar, status\\n  bar, or row should use one baseline or center line instead of individually\\n  tuned offsets.\\n- Introduce indentation only for real hierarchy, containment, or disclosure.\\n  Decorative indentation makes siblings look subordinate and breaks the\\n  surface's reading line.\\n- When a nested level ends, return exactly to the parent spine. Do not let\\n  accumulated padding drift across nested containers.\\n- Preserve the spine through optional content. Missing icons, badges,\\n  descriptions, or trailing actions must not move the remaining labels; use\\n  intentional slots or lanes when cross-row comparison matters.\\n- Align major regions with one another where their hierarchy matches. Sidebar\\n  headers, content titles, split panes, toolbars, and bottom bars need not share\\n  every coordinate, but coincident levels should form visible continuous lines.\\n\\nNot every edge should align. A child can indent, a primary value can lead its\\nsupporting metadata, and a destructive decision can gain separation. Such\\nexceptions must communicate hierarchy or meaning; they must not result from\\nuncoordinated component padding. Start with the shared spine, then make the\\nexception explicit.\\n\\nTreat exact alignment and repeated gaps as quality invariants. When two edges\\nor spaces are intended to be equal, a one-rendered-pixel difference is a defect,\\nnot an acceptable optical approximation. Inspect resolved bounds with a\\nmeasurement tool at representative window sizes, zoom levels, and display scale\\nfactors.
